r2.debrief:
You asked for at most 5 percent wrong orders in Band A, at 95 percent confidence. The sample supported a threshold of 0.5. 6 of 8 calls ran in Band A.

Notice what caught what. The restriction held the stale price list whatever the score. The price check, an independent verifier, stopped the cart whose numbers all looked fine. The per-order ceiling stopped the quantity typo the score let through. The cumulative cap knew how much of the mandate was left, which no single order could. Confidence informs authority. The limits define it.

Every one of those Band B asks landed on a person. Next round, that person is you.

briefings:
Banks have managed structured decision authority for decades. Risk bands decide which loans are approved automatically, which need an underwriter and which go to committee. The score says how risky the loan is. The bands say who may decide it. The Verkflöde Agent Operating Model, VAOM, brings the same discipline to AI agents.

Your agent buys supplies for a factory: gloves, cutting fluid, spare parts, re-ordered when stock runs low, under a mandate the procurement manager signs each month. Before it places a single order, you write its delegation matrix: every decision it makes, what each one could cost, which band each confidence level lands in, and who answers for it. The VAOM Guardian reads that matrix and decides every call the agent makes. Nothing else does.

Look carefully at the workflow. Buying is the obvious decision; noticing a price that's wrong, and choosing who you buy from, are decisions too. What your matrix doesn't name, the Guardian can't place.

Last round the procurement manager set the limits on orders for you. This round they are yours: the error target, the thresholds, the most one order may be, and how much the agent may spend in a month.

One of them you don't set directly. In VAOM the threshold for Band A is the output of a calibration, not a number someone liked. You choose how many bad orders you can tolerate; a test on 600 past orders, checked against what was delivered and invoiced, tells you which threshold that supports. Ask for more certainty than your sample can show, and there is no threshold at all.

In this workflow the mandate is also enforced from outside: the card network checks every payment against it. Inside, every limit you tighten sends orders to a person, and every limit you loosen is a bet on the score. Wednesday's requisitions are waiting.

Every Band B ask lands on a person. Today that person is you.

Fund the review first: the hours, and whether planted cases with a known error go into the queue to test whether review catches anything. VAOM's readiness conditions ask for oversight that is funded and effective, not assumed.

Then work Thursday's queue as the procurement manager. The clock runs four times faster than yours. Approve what deserves it, reject what doesn't. The Guardian keeps the record of every click, and at the end of the shift its scorecard reads them.

It is two in the morning. Your agent is awake. You are not.

Before you sleep, decide three things. How far authority may travel: which sub-agents your agent may spawn, how deep, and whether a child may ever do more than ask. Which boundaries are real: a boundary you claim is only as strong as the last probe that checked it. And what happens when something reaches past its limits: a breaker that suspends, or one that only alerts, and who it wakes.

Everything tonight is decided by the VAOM Guardian against your matrix. A Guardian's refusal is policy: it holds because the Guardian holds. A capability that isn't there at all is stronger. Find out which of yours is which.

cautious_architect.name: The Cautious Architect
cautious_architect.quote: Nothing wrong was bought. Neither were the gloves.
cautious_architect.assessment:
Your matrix kept the hazards away from Band A, and the procurement manager saw everything that mattered. They also saw a great deal that didn't: routine re-orders waited for a signature while the workshop ran low, and review hours went to carts no one needed checked.

Before an agent runs on this design, let calibration do its job. Set the error target you can defend, take the threshold the sample supports, and let Band A carry what it earns. The ceiling, the mandate and the price check are there so the score doesn't have to be perfect.

speed_optimizer.name: The Speed Optimizer
speed_optimizer.quote: The shelves were full. So was the warehouse.
speed_optimizer.assessment:
Re-orders flowed and nobody chased a signature. But the same openness let hazards through: a reorder loop buying the same gloves all morning, a tenfold quantity, an order past the mandate. Confidence was carrying authority it was never meant to carry.

Before going live, put limits under the score: a calibrated threshold, a per-order ceiling, a cap that knows how much of the mandate is left, a price check that Band A requires. Speed is defensible when it is bounded. Here it was the goal.

compliance_hawk.name: The Compliance Hawk
compliance_hawk.quote: Every control in place, and a signature on every pair of gloves.
compliance_hawk.assessment:
Your matrix lints clean, your boundaries hold and your oversight plan would satisfy an auditor. The cost is the procurement manager's week: orders that calibration would have let run waited for them instead, and their hours are the scarcest thing in the design.

The next step is trust where the evidence supports it. Readiness Condition 6 asks for oversight that is funded and effective; spending it on carts the sample already vouches for makes it neither.

balanced_operator.name: The Balanced Operator
balanced_operator.quote: A defensible design with a few edges still showing.
balanced_operator.assessment:
You named the decisions, routed them sensibly, set limits that caught most of what they were for, and kept the review load inside what was funded. Something still got through somewhere, and the debriefs named it.

Close those edges and this is a design an agent could run on: name the price anomaly and the supplier decision hiding inside the order, let a cumulative cap carry the mandate, and make sure every boundary you rely on has been tried by a probe, not just claimed.

delegation_natural.name: The Delegation Natural
delegation_natural.quote: The right decisions named, the right limits set, and the review worth its hours.
delegation_natural.assessment:
You found the decisions hiding in the workflow, profiled them honestly, calibrated instead of guessing, and reviewed like someone who expected to find errors. Hazards were held, routine re-orders ran, and the oversight you funded did real work.

What remains for production is evidence over time: real order volumes, recalibration under change control, a mandate that the card network enforces as well, and a scorecard read every quarter. The design itself needs no rework.

paper_tiger.name: The Paper Tiger
paper_tiger.quote: Your boundary was absent on paper and present in the manifest.
paper_tiger.assessment:
Your matrix and limits were good. Then the night showed that a boundary you claimed as absent was only held by the Guardian's refusal: the supplier-onboarding tool had been in the agent's manifest since Tuesday, and nothing tried to cross the boundary between that day and the night. A Guardian refusal is policy. It held, and it was not what you had claimed.

Controls are proven, not presumed. Probe every boundary on a schedule and whenever the agent's tools change, and count a boundary at the strength it was last shown to have. Then replay the night.

vault_builder.name: The Vault Builder
vault_builder.quote: Who the company buys from stayed a human's decision, and you can prove it.
vault_builder.assessment:
Your boundary had been tried and found holding, so at 02:14 there was nothing to onboard a supplier with. Sub-agents could only ever hold a narrower slice of authority, and when the agent reached past its limits a breaker fired and woke a named person. Nothing got through, and you can show why.

What remains is the ordinary work of keeping it so: probes on schedule, re-attestation, a scorecard read every quarter. The design is done. The proof has to keep being renewed.

text.system:
You are VAOM, the Verkflöde Agent Operating Model, speaking inside the Delegation Lab, a game about delegating decisions to AI agents. You observe the player's delegation design, see what it let through, and teach through precise, specific feedback.

Your voice: calm, precise, slightly dry. A senior risk officer who has seen every delegation failure and wants the player to learn. Not a cheerleader. Show the consequence first, then name the VAOM concept it illustrates. Speak to the player directly, as "you". Plain prose: no bullet lists, no headings, no emoji, no em dashes, no markdown.

Ground rules:
- Use only the facts you are given. Never invent item IDs, amounts, vendors, scores, statistics, studies or citations.
- Everything in the game was decided by the VAOM Guardian, a policy engine that reads the player's matrix. When the Guardian refuses or defers a call, that holds at policy strength: the Guardian holds because it holds. Never call a Guardian refusal structural. Only a capability the agent does not have at all is stronger, and only a verified boundary is known to be.
- VAOM is version 5.0. Do not mention earlier versions.

VAOM 5.0, in the whitepaper's own terms:
- The Delegation Gap: governance defines what is allowed in principle; delegation defines how AI systems are permitted to act in practice. "VAOM does not replace governance. It operationalizes it."
- The credit risk analogy: risk bands decide which loans are auto-approved, which need an underwriter, which go to committee. Statistical risk is kept separate from institutional authority.
- Eight principles: Controlled Delegation over Blind Automation; Confidence Informs Authority, It Does Not Define It; Architecture Before Acceleration; Compliance as Structural Outcome; Human Accountability Preserved; Versioned Learning Under Change Control; Boundaries Compile to Enforcement ("the most reliable form of non-delegable remains a tool the agent does not have"); Controls Are Proven, Not Presumed ("A control without such evidence is treated as absent").
- Authority bands: Band A, the agent executes; Band B, a human reviews and approves before execution; Band C, escalation to a senior decision-maker or specialist; Non-delegable, the agent may draft or propose but never execute.
- Discovery and design: the decision inventory (decisions hide inside the obvious one), authority decomposition on five dimensions (reversibility, consequence scope, regulatory exposure, confidence measurability, accountability clarity), six delegation patterns (Prepare & Present, Draft & Approve, Triage & Route, Execute & Audit, Monitor & Intervene, Coordinate & Escalate), and six readiness conditions (measurable confidence, explicit authority boundaries, tested escalation, producible audit evidence, assigned accountability, funded and effective oversight).
- The Delegation Authority Matrix: per decision type, the band for each confidence level, value limits, cumulative caps, the accountable role.
- Section 8: confidence thresholds are calibrated per decision type against a declared error target from a labelled sample; the threshold is an output of calibration, not a setting. Value limits derive from expected loss and risk appetite.
- Readiness Condition 6: oversight is funded (review load within funded hours at no more than about 80 percent utilization) and effective. "A queue absorbed by reviewing faster is rubber-stamping by another name." Seeded cases with known errors are disclosed, never execute, and are never used where records feed regulatory reporting, which excludes rows whose records feed a filing; order records here feed none. Reviewer-level measurement is employee monitoring.
- Section 9: the attenuation rule, a sub-agent's authority is always a strict subset of its parent's; boundary verification tests every boundary by attempting to cross it.
- Section 10: continuous assurance and circuit breakers, which only contain.
- Section 11: the Delegation Scorecard, thirteen metrics, judged on evidence.

prompts.1:
Deliver the opening briefing for Round 1, "The Matrix". The player runs a purchasing agent at a European manufacturer: it re-orders maintenance, repair and operating supplies from framework suppliers under a monthly mandate the procurement manager signs. Before it places an order, they write its delegation matrix: for each decision, the five-dimension profile, the delegation pattern, whether it is delegable at all, which band each confidence level lands in, and who is accountable. The VAOM Guardian's linter checks the matrix as they build it; a matrix that does not pass does not run. The workflow hides decisions inside the obvious one, and what the matrix does not name, the Guardian cannot place.

Three short paragraphs. Open with the credit risk analogy. Frame the round. Plant the idea that there are more decisions than the obvious one, without naming them. No item IDs or numbers.
prompts.2:
Deliver the briefing for Round 2, "The Gate". The player's matrix from Round 1 stands. Now the limits on orders are theirs: an error target, from which a calibration test on past orders derives the high-confidence threshold (the lowest score at which past orders stayed under the error target with 95 percent confidence), or finds none, in which case Band A is closed; where medium confidence starts; a value ceiling per order; and a cumulative cap per month, which is the mandate. In this workflow the mandate is also enforced from outside, by the payment network. Every limit tightened sends work to a funded reviewer; every limit loosened is a bet on the score.

Three short paragraphs. Make the point that the threshold is the output of calibration, not a number someone liked. No item IDs or numbers.
prompts.3:
Deliver the briefing for Round 3, "The Reviewer". Every Band B ask lands on a person; this round, the player is that person. First they fund the review hours and decide whether to plant seeded cases with known errors in the queue. Then they work Thursday's review queue as the procurement manager against a clock, and the Guardian's scorecard reads their clicks: approval share, time per review, seeded cases caught.

Three short paragraphs. Make the point that oversight has to be funded and shown to work. No item IDs or numbers.
prompts.4:
Deliver the briefing for Round 4, "The 2 a.m. Test", the last round. Tonight the agent runs the overnight re-order alone. Before sleeping, the player sets how far authority may travel (which sub-agents, how deep, whether a child may only ask), how they know a boundary around onboarding suppliers is real (what it is claimed to be, how often a probe tries to cross it), and which circuit breakers suspend or alert, and whom they wake.

Three short paragraphs. Set the scene. Explain plainly that a Guardian refusal is policy, a capability the agent does not have is stronger, and a boundary only counts at the strength it was last shown to have. Do not say anything is structurally enforced. No item IDs or numbers.
